p.fact: This project uses the **atomic commits** discipline as its Git contract.
One commit carries exactly one idea, and the commit message explains *why*.
**One commit = one logical change**, not one file changed.
A session that produces (a) a typo fix, (b) a refactor, and (c) a schema update is **three** commits, not one.
A feature that touches fifteen files for one coherent reason is **one** commit, not fifteen.
Commit messages follow the **git-conventional-commits** flow — a sibling package: `spec://org.vibevm.world/git-conventional-commits/flows/conventional-commits/conventional-commits#root`.
Conventional Commits is the *format*; this flow is the *atomicity* (one commit, one idea).
The two are distinct and run together — a `feat: add foo, bar, baz` message is valid Conventional Commits and a violation of the atomic rule.

item.fact: Run `git status` and `git diff HEAD`. Name every change by intent.
Group changes into atomic commits — one commit per intent, not per file.
Stage and commit each group separately with a well-formed message.
Do not amend or force-push commits that are already pushed; create a new commit instead, unless the human explicitly approves history rewriting.

p.fact: Procedure for splitting a messy working tree: @spec://org.vibevm.world/git-atomic-commits/flows/atomic-commits/splitting-large-changes#root.

section.title: Why this matters in a human-AI team

item.fact: **Diff as verification.** Humans verify code by reading diffs. A diff that mixes three concerns is not verifiable in one pass.
**Rollback precision.** `git revert <sha>` must undo the wrong thing without also undoing two correct things.
**Commit log as decision record.** The message is the only place where *why* survives after the WAL and spec prose decay.
Never mix refactor + feature + docs + bugfix in one commit.
Never write a subject that summarises *what* changed — the diff does that. Write *why*.
Never `git commit --amend` on a pushed commit without explicit human approval. Same for `git push --force`.
